title: A table has grown too big — what do you do?
summary: "Too big" means two different problems — slow queries and expensive storage. Learn to name concrete remedies for each instead of reaching for read replicas by default.

slides.markdown:
"Too big" is ambiguous, and answering it well starts by resolving that ambiguity. A table can be too big in two distinct ways: queries against it have gotten slow, or storing it has gotten expensive — and these two problems have different fixes.

A table that's slow because every query scans a huge range needs partitioning or sharding. A table that's expensive because it holds years of rarely-touched history needs archiving. Conflating the two, or reaching for one fix regardless of which problem you actually have, is the trap this question sets.

Ask: **is the pain slow queries, expensive storage, or both — and is the old data still accessed?** A table with terrible query latency but cheap storage needs a very different fix from one that's fast to query but costly to keep around.

Also ask how the data is actually queried: do users need last week's rows constantly, but data from two years ago almost never? That access pattern is exactly what determines whether archiving is safe, or whether "old" data is still load-bearing and needs to stay hot.

Structure it as: **partition or shard for query speed; archive cold data for storage cost; apply both if both are hurting.** These are independent levers — partitioning doesn't reduce storage cost by itself, and archiving doesn't speed up queries against the data you keep hot.

"If queries scanning this table are slow, I'd partition by a natural axis like time. If the real problem is storage cost from years of rarely-accessed history, I'd archive that history to cheaper storage instead — or do both if the table is genuinely hurting on both fronts."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: partitioning an events table by month
slides.markdown:
An events table queried almost entirely for "this month's events" benefits directly from **partitioning by month**: each partition holds one month's rows, and a query scoped to the current month only ever touches that one partition, never scanning the other 23 months alongside it.

This is a pure query-speed fix — the total data stored doesn't shrink, but the amount any single query has to scan does, often dramatically. It solves the "queries are slow" half of "too big" without touching the "storage is expensive" half at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: archiving cold data with a rehydration path
slides.markdown:
For the storage-cost half, archive rows past a retention window — say, older than a year — out of the primary table and into cheaper storage (a data warehouse, a blob store, a colder database tier). The primary table shrinks, and so does its backup size, replication cost, and index maintenance overhead.

Crucially, keep a **rehydration path**: a documented, if slower, way to pull an archived row back if it's ever needed unexpectedly. Archiving without a way back turns a cost optimization into permanent data loss the first time someone genuinely needs an old record.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the thresholds that should trigger this conversation early
slides.markdown:
Name concrete numbers rather than waiting for an incident: a table crossing tens of millions of rows, or query latency on it climbing past a defined SLO (say, p99 over 200ms for a previously-fast lookup), or its portion of total storage cost crossing a noticeable share of the infrastructure bill.

Treating these as trigger points for a proactive conversation — before the table becomes the thing paging someone at 3am — is the difference between a planned partitioning project and an emergency one done under pressure with a much smaller margin for error.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this explicitly: **archiving cuts cost hard, but makes old-data queries slower and more complex — decide who actually needs that data and how fast, before archiving it away.** It's not a free win; it's a bet that the old data's access frequency is low enough to justify the retrieval cost when it is needed.

A compliance team needing seven-year-old records for an audit, retrieved once a year, tolerates a slow rehydration path fine. A support team needing to look up a six-month-old order during a live customer call does not — naming which case you're in changes the whole design.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a report needs both hot and archived data
slides.markdown:
Name the pattern: query the hot table for recent data and the archive store for older data, then merge the two result sets in the application or reporting layer — since there's typically no single query that spans both systems natively. This is slower and more complex than a single query, which is exactly the cost archiving imposes on cross-boundary reports.

For a report run often enough to matter, consider a scheduled job that pre-aggregates across both sources into a separate summary table, so the expensive cross-source merge happens once on a schedule instead of on every report request.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how did nobody notice until it was this big?
slides.markdown:
Name concrete monitoring you'd add: alerting on table row-count growth rate and total size, not just absolute thresholds, so a sudden acceleration in growth (a new feature writing far more rows than expected) gets caught early. Also track query latency trends on the table's hot paths over time, since gradual degradation is easy to miss day-to-day but obvious on a month-over-month graph.

The honest answer to "how did nobody notice" is usually "nobody was watching a trend, only a point-in-time metric" — naming that gap, and the trend-based monitoring that fixes it, is the real answer here.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adding read replicas to fix a size problem
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Queries against this table are slow — let's add more read replicas."

**Why it's wrong:** read replicas help when the bottleneck is read *volume* — too many concurrent readers overwhelming one instance. They do nothing for a query that's slow because it has to scan an enormous amount of data on every single execution, regardless of how many replicas share that same scan cost.

**Correct model:** diagnose whether the problem is read volume (replicas help) or query cost from table size and layout (partitioning, indexing, or archiving help) before picking a fix — they solve different problems.

"'Too big' means two different things, so I'd ask which one: slow queries or expensive storage. Slow queries usually mean partitioning by a natural axis like time, so a query scoped to a recent range never scans the rest. Expensive storage usually means archiving cold data to cheaper storage, with a rehydration path in case it's ever needed. I'd apply one, the other, or both, but I wouldn't reach for read replicas unless the actual problem is read volume, not table size or layout."
